title: Working Scientifically
seo_title: Year 9 Science: Working Scientifically Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_code: AC9S9I01, AC9S9I02, AC9S9I03, AC9S9I04, AC9S9I05, AC9S9I06, AC9S9I07, AC9S9I08
standard_text: Develop investigable questions and hypotheses; plan and conduct safe, ethical and valid investigations; process data using means, ranges, rates and percentage change; analyse uncertainty and errors; evaluate sources, claims and methods; and communicate evidence-based conclusions (summary of the Australian Curriculum v9.0 Year 9 science inquiry content descriptions).
meta_desc: Free Year 9 science worksheets on working scientifically: hypotheses, control groups, ethics, means and uncertainty, rates from data, percentage change, errors and evaluating sources. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Report the mean with its uncertainty.
key_sub: Repeat trials, calculate a mean and report uncertainty as half the range.
body_html:
How to think about it

Good investigations are valid, reliable and ethical.

  • A testable hypothesis names the variables and gives a reason. A control group allows a fair comparison.
  • Process data: mean, range, uncertainty (± half the range), rate = change ÷ time, percentage change = change ÷ original × 100.
  • Evaluate: random and systematic errors, sample size, bias, peer review and whether the data really supports the conclusion.
Example

Results 3.1, 3.3, 3.2, 3.2 s. Mean ± uncertainty?

mean 3.2

range 0.2, half is 0.1

Answer: 3.2 ± 0.1 s

Example

Seedlings 40 → 50. Percentage increase?

10 ÷ 40 × 100

Answer: 25%

Common mistakes

  • Using the range or the total instead of the mean.
  • Saying one experiment 'proves' a hypothesis.
  • Trusting a source because it is popular rather than peer reviewed.

faq.a: Find the range of the repeated results (largest − smallest) and halve it. Report the mean ± this value, such as 4.2 ± 0.1 s.

faq.q: What is the difference between random and systematic errors?
faq.a: Random errors make readings vary unpredictably; repeating and averaging helps. Systematic errors shift every reading the same way; calibrating equipment fixes them.

faq.q: Why does ethics matter in science?
faq.a: Investigations must protect people, animals and the environment. People must give informed consent, and animal studies need ethics approval.

items.q: In an experiment, the number of bacteria colonies after adding antiseptic changed from 40 to 30. What is the percentage decrease?
items.e: Percentage change = change ÷ original × 100 = 10 ÷ 40 × 100 = 25%.

items.q: Liam uses a data logger to record the temperature every second. What is the main advantage?
c: more frequent and precise readings without reaction-time error
items.e: Technology improves data collection.

items.q: Which source is most reliable for a science report?
items.e: Peer review means other experts checked it.

items.q: What does 'reproducible' mean?
c: other scientists get the same results when they repeat the method
items.e: Clear methods make results reproducible.

items.q: Why should graphs have the independent variable on the x-axis?
c: it is the convention, so the graph shows how the dependent variable changes with it
items.e: The dependent variable goes on the y-axis.

items.q: A group repeated a test of the time for a trolley to roll down a ramp four times: 2.1 s, 2.4 s, 2.4 s, 2.7 s. What is the mean?
items.e: Add the results and divide by 4: 9.6 ÷ 4 = 2.4 s.

items.q: In an experiment, the height of a seedling changed from 120 mm to 144 mm. What is the percentage increase?
items.e: Percentage change = change ÷ original × 100 = 24 ÷ 120 × 100 = 20%.

items.q: What makes an experiment valid?
c: it tests what it is meant to test, with all other variables controlled

items.q: Ruby's data have a large range between trials. What should she do?
c: repeat the trials and look for sources of random error
items.e: A large range means low precision.

items.q: In an experiment, the mass of a plant over two weeks changed from 80 g to 88 g. What is the percentage increase?
items.e: Percentage change = change ÷ original × 100 = 8 ÷ 80 × 100 = 10%.

items.q: In an experiment, the height of a seedling changed from 120 mm to 150 mm. What is the percentage increase?
items.e: Percentage change = change ÷ original × 100 = 30 ÷ 120 × 100 = 25%.

items.q: A survey asks only students at one surf club about their favourite sport. Which change would best improve the investigation?
c: Give every pot the same amount of water.
Repeat the trial to see if the result happens again.
Use the same beaker and volume of water.
Survey a random sample from many schools.
items.e: The sample is not representative of all students.

items.q: Kai reads a news story that says a new food 'cures' colds. What should he check first?
c: whether the claim is based on peer-reviewed research with a large sample
items.e: Good evidence comes from controlled studies.

items.q: Zara's results support her hypothesis. Can she say it is proven?
c: Yes, if the graph is neat.
No, the data support it, but more testing could change our understanding.
items.e: Science is open to new evidence.
